screens.title: Introduction to Podman and Rootless Containers
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will explore Podman, a daemonless container engine that runs containers as regular user processes and embraces the OCI standards. We'll show why Podman's architecture matters for security and resilience, how rootless containers limit exposure of host root, and how common workflow tasks—pulling images, running containers, building images, and using multi-service compose files—map to Podman commands. You will see a short hands-on plan you can use on a CentOS or Fedora-style system: install Podman, verify the rootless configuration, run a simple Nginx container without sudo, build an image from a Dockerfile, and deploy a compose file with podman-compose. We'll also cover the small but important system files that enable rootless mapping and common troubleshooting steps if mappings are missing. By the end you will understand the architectural contrast with Docker, have a repeatable set of commands to try in a lab, and be able to explain why running containers without a central root daemon reduces the attack surface. Think about how running containers as your own user changes how you grant privileges and manage lifecycle on multi-user systems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you will develop a compact but practical skill set for working with Podman in an LFCE context. First, you'll learn to distinguish Podman's daemonless architecture from Docker's daemon-based model, and explain why that reduces a single point of failure and the daemon attack surface. Second, you'll install Podman on a Linux host, configure and verify a rootless environment using subuid and subgid mappings, and interpret the output of diagnostic commands. Third, you'll perform core container lifecycle tasks: pulling images, running containers, listing and stopping containers, removing containers and images, and executing into running containers for troubleshooting. Fourth, you'll build a container image from a Dockerfile using podman build and deploy multi-container applications with podman-compose in a rootless context. Each objective focuses on practical commands and common pitfalls so you can apply these skills in a lab or production-like environment and explain trade-offs to a systems team.

screens.title: Podman vs Docker — daemonless architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Let's make a precise comparison you can use during troubleshooting or in a design discussion. Docker uses a central daemon — dockerd — that runs as a privileged service and manages all containers for the host. Podman, in contrast, is daemonless: it runs commands that interact directly with kernel facilities and manages containers as user processes, each monitored by a small conmon helper. The practical security result is important: with Docker a vulnerability in dockerd could affect all containers and escalate privileges because dockerd runs with elevated rights. With Podman, containers run under the initiating user's namespace. That means if a container is compromised, the attacker only gains the privileges of that mapped user rather than the host root. A concrete example: on a shared developer workstation, multiple users can run their own rootless containers without a single root-owned daemon controlling them. A common misconception is that rootless equals fully safe; it's not. Rootless reduces host-level exposure, but image vulnerabilities and user-level data access can still cause harm. Your takeaway: when you argue for Podman in a secure environment, emphasize reduced attack surface and per-user isolation, but also advise continued image hygiene and least privilege practices.

keyIdea.text: Podman's daemonless model and per-container monitoring reduce scope for a single privileged process to compromise multiple containers.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Daemonless Architecture
Core Claim

Daemonless design reduces privileged attack surface

Podman manages containers as normal user processes with conmon monitoring, while Docker relies on a privileged dockerd daemon. This architecture changes how failures and exploits propagate.

Podman: no long-running root daemon; per-user containers.
Docker: dockerd runs as a service and manages all containers centrally.
Result: fewer host-level privileges required for everyday container lifecycle tasks.
Example Scenario
On a multi-user build server, Alice and Bob run their own rootless containers with Podman. A vulnerable image exploited in Alice's container cannot directly compromise the host root or Bob's containers because namespaces and subuid mappings isolate processes to each user.
Common misconception: Rootless eliminates all risk — it reduces but does not remove risks from insecure images or privileged mounts.
Side-by-side
Docker
  • Central dockerd service
  • Daemon runs with elevated privileges
  • Single point for lifecycle management
Podman
  • No persistent daemon
  • Containers are user processes
  • Conmon monitors each container
Key Takeaway

Daemonless operation narrows the escalation path by avoiding a single privileged daemon, but maintain image and runtime hygiene to minimize risk.

screens.title: Rootless Containers and UID/GID Mapping
screens.narratorSegment: Rootless containers let non-root users run containers without requiring sudo or membership in a docker group. The mechanism that makes this possible is user namespace mapping: the kernel maps a range of subordinate UIDs and GIDs to the non-root user's namespace so that processes inside the container can appear as root while the mapped UIDs on the host are non-privileged. On most distributions those mappings are configured in two files: /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid. Each line assigns a starting UID and a range to a user. A concrete example is adding the line that maps one hundred thousand UIDs to your account so Podman can map container root to those host UIDs. You will verify rootless operation with a diagnostic such as podman info --debug that reports rootless true. A common misstep is forgetting to log out and back in after editing subuid/subgid so the kernel mappings take effect for your session. Another mistake is assuming rootless always means the container runs as your host user inside; inside the container the user might still be root, but that root is namespaced and mapped to a non-root account on the host. Takeaway: subuid/subgid mapping is small to configure but vital to enable safe rootless workflows.

keyIdea.title: Namespaced root via subuid/subgid
keyIdea.text: subuid and subgid map a range of host IDs to your user so container root is namespaced and doesn't equate to host root.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Rootless Containers
What rootless means

Rootless containers let you run container workloads without granting host root to the container runtime. Instead, Podman maps a range of UIDs/GIDs so container root maps to non-privileged host IDs.

Configuration files
# /etc/subuid (example)
alice:100000:65536
# /etc/subgid (example)
alice:100000:65536
After adding these lines for your user, re-login so the new subordinate ID ranges are available to your session and Podman can use them.
Verify
Run the Podman debug info command shown in the exercise to confirm it reports rootless mode and shows the ID mappings.
Common Mistake
Editing subuid/subgid without a re-login or missing the entry will prevent rootless containers from starting and lead to UID mapping errors.
Why it matters
Subuid/subgid mappings enable per-user isolation on shared systems, reducing the chance that a container compromise affects the host root account.

screens.title: Installing Podman and verifying rootless setup
screens.narratorSegment: This screen gives you a concise install and verification process you can run during a live lab. First, install Podman from your distribution repositories using the package manager for your system. On CentOS Stream or Fedora-family systems the package is available and the install step is a single privileged command. Second, check for an entry for your username in /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid. If entries are missing, add a subordinate range for both files and re-login. Third, run the Podman diagnostic in debug mode to confirm Podman is operating rootless. That diagnostic output is your proof for a lab exercise: it will show a line indicating rootless true and display the ID mapping ranges. A practical tip is to create the subuid/subgid entries with the same numeric range for both files so mapping is symmetrical. A common troubleshooting step after editing the files is to log out and back in, because the kernel mapping information is applied at session start. Finally, if you need podman-compose later, install the package from the repository as well so you can use existing Compose files. This checklist keeps the number of steps minimal and repeatable during an exam environment.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Install & Verify
Install

Install from your distribution's default repository so package updates and dependencies are managed by the system package manager.

sudo dnf install podman -y
Note: The install step requires privileges, but running containers can be done rootless after configuration.
Verify mapping
Ensure /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid contain entries for your user. If missing, add a range and re-login so mappings apply.
Diagnostic
podman info --debug | grep -i "rootless"
A returned value indicating rootless true confirms your session is configured correctly.
Install podman-compose
If you plan to run Compose files, install podman-compose from the repos so you can reuse docker-compose.yml files in a rootless environment.
Check your understanding

Why is logging out and back in required after editing subuid/subgid? Consider the kernel and session mapping lifecycle.

screens.title: Core Podman commands — terminal demo
screens.narratorSegment: In this walkthrough you'll see the core Podman commands you will run repeatedly. The Podman CLI is largely compatible with Docker, so workflows transfer quickly. Practically, you will pull an image from a registry, run a container detached and map a port, list running containers, stop and remove containers, and execute a shell inside a running container for inspection. An example workflow is pulling the latest nginx image, running it in detached mode with a host port forwarded to container port 80, confirming the container is running with the ps command, and using exec to run whoami inside to observe the mapped user inside the container. A common misconception is that the absence of sudo in these commands means less capability; actually, when running rootless, the container's root is namespaced to your subordinate UID range. The example code panel contains the exact commands you can paste into a lab terminal. After you practice these commands, you should be able to show a running rootless web server reachable on a forwarded host port and provide podman ps output as proof. Core Podman commands — terminal demo means podman's commands look like docker's but run under your user namespace when rootless, giving the same actions with lower host-level privileges.. In practical terms, pulling, running, listing, stopping, removing, and exec into containers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Core Commands
Terminal commands

Use these commands to perform basic container lifecycle operations with Podman. They map closely to Docker equivalents.

podman pull nginx:latest
podman run -d --name my-nginx -p 8080:80 nginx:latest
podman ps
podman ps -a
podman stop my-nginx
podman rm my-nginx
podman exec -it my-nginx bash
podman images
podman rmi nginx:latest
These commands will run without sudo when your rootless mapping is configured. Use podman ps and podman images to inspect runtime state and local images.
Concrete example
Run nginx, forward host 8080, and verify through podman ps and by browsing http://localhost:8080 on the host.
Misconception
Don't assume rootless containers have no mapping between container root and host; the container root is present inside the namespace but mapped to non-root host IDs.
Key Takeaway
Podman offers the same operational commands you're used to, but privileges are bound to the user's namespace when rootless.

screens.title: Building images with Podman
screens.narratorSegment: Building container images is a frequent task in an LFCE lab or production pipeline. Podman supports building images from Dockerfiles with a nearly identical command to Docker, so you can reuse existing Dockerfiles. The typical flow is: create a Dockerfile, run the build command with a tag, and then run the resulting image. A concrete example included here uses a small Alpine-based image that installs cowsay and prints a message at runtime. The build is performed locally and the resulting image can be run without requiring a privileged daemon. A common misunderstanding is thinking podman build requires different Dockerfile syntax; it does not. Dockerfile directives and layers behave the same because Podman is OCI-compliant. When building rootless, be mindful of file ownership on the host; files created by build processes may be owned by mapped UIDs. The example code block is safe to paste into a lab terminal. After building, run the image to confirm behavior and then clean up images and containers to avoid leftover artifacts. This workflow demonstrates how Podman enables image creation without a persistent root process.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Build Images
Create a simple Dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM alpine:latest
RUN apk add --no-cache cowsay
CMD ["cowsay", "Moo from Podman!"]
Build the image using podman build and tag it so you can run it locally with podman run. The same Dockerfile works unchanged.
Build & run
podman build -t my-cow-app:latest .
podman run my-cow-app:latest
Note: When run rootless, the container runs in your user namespace; inside the container the user may be root, but that root is mapped to non-root host IDs.
Concrete example
Build the cowsay image and run it to see the output, then use podman images and podman ps to confirm artifacts.
Common Mistake
Forgetting to tag the image makes it harder to reference and remove later; use a clear tag like my-cow-app:latest.
Key Takeaway
podman build is compatible with existing Dockerfiles, letting you build images without a central daemon.

screens.title: podman-compose for multi-container applications
screens.narratorSegment: If your application uses multiple services defined in a docker-compose. yml file, podman-compose lets you bring those services up and down with familiar commands. Install the podman-compose package, then run podman-compose up -d to start services in detached mode and podman-compose down to stop them. The tool reads the existing Compose file and orchestrates containers using Podman rather than Docker. A concrete example is bringing up a web service and a database defined in a Compose file; podman-compose will create the necessary networks and start containers under rootless mappings if your session is configured. A common misconception is believing every Compose feature is supported identically; while most standard Compose files work, advanced Compose extensions or specific volume drivers may differ. Also be mindful of host port collisions when running multiple user sessions on the same host. The key benefit is workflow continuity: teams can migrate Compose-based deployments to a rootless Podman environment with minimal changes, retaining familiar multi-container orchestration without a central root daemon. podman-compose for multi-container applications means podman-compose reads standard docker-compose.yml files and orchestrates multi-container apps in a rootless podman environment.. In practical terms, reuse existing docker-compose.yml files in a rootless podman environment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › podman-compose
Install and run a Compose stack
Install podman-compose and reuse your existing Compose files to deploy multi-container applications without Docker.
sudo dnf install podman-compose -y
podman-compose up -d
podman-compose down
Concrete Example
Bring up a web service and a database defined in docker-compose.yml and confirm services are running with podman ps.
Caveat
Some Compose extensions and third-party drivers may not translate perfectly; test Compose files before relying on them in production.
Try this

Use podman-compose up -d with a simple two-service compose file and verify both services are accessible on their forwarded ports.

screens.title: Podman's runtime components and conmon
screens.narratorSegment: Podman's runtime is composed of several small programs rather than a single daemon. One of these is conmon, a container monitor used to track container processes, forward logs, and collect exit codes. In practice, when you start a container with Podman, a conmon process is launched to supervise that container's runtime. Podman also interacts with kernel features such as cgroups and namespaces directly for resource and isolation controls. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Runtime Components
conmon and the runtime

Podman launches a small monitor process named conmon for each container. Conmon handles logging, exit codes, and lifecycle supervision without a central daemon.

Per-container supervisor: conmon
Direct kernel interactions: namespaces and cgroups
No single privileged daemon to manage all containers
Why this matters
Isolated supervision reduces blast radius when a single container has runtime problems and makes per-user lifecycle management straightforward.
Common Misunderstanding
Conmon does not add privileges to containers; it simply supervises processes and collects logs and exit codes.
Key Takeaway
Small supervisory processes plus kernel namespaces give Podman resilience without a central privileged service.

screens.title: Systemd integration for user services
screens.narratorSegment: Podman integrates smoothly with systemd, enabling you to manage container lifecycles as user services. Because Podman is daemonless and can run in user mode, you can create a systemd user unit file that starts a container at login or on boot for that user. The typical unit specifies ExecStart that runs podman run or podman start, and systemd will supervise the unit under the user's systemd instance. This is particularly useful for per-user services that must persist across sessions or auto-start after a reboot without root-level systemd units. A concrete example is generating a unit with podman generate systemd --name my-container which helps create a template systemd service for that container. A common misconception is expecting system-wide systemd behavior; user units live in the user's scope and do not equate to system services. For administration, this approach offers robust lifecycle controls and logging from systemd while maintaining per-user namespace boundaries. Reflect: consider when you would prefer a user unit over central system-level management for multi-tenant environments. Systemd integration for user services means use systemd user services to auto-start and supervise podman containers per user without root-level system services.. In practical terms, managing podman containers with systemd user units. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Systemd Integration
Why use systemd user units?

You can auto-start and supervise containers per user, integrate logs into the systemd journal, and manage restart policies without creating system-level services.

# Example generator command
podman generate systemd --name my-container --files --new
The generator helps create a unit you can enable in your user systemd instance.
Concrete Use
Enable a user-level unit to restart a container after user login or system reboot, keeping services scoped to the owning user.
Misconception
User systemd units do not provide system-wide service guarantees; they operate in the user's login/session context.
Key Takeaway
Systemd user integration gives robust lifecycle control while preserving per-user isolation inherent to Podman.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When working with Podman in rootless mode, you will encounter a small number of recurring setup and runtime issues. First, missing or incorrect subuid/subgid entries lead to UID mapping errors; the symptom is container creation failures or explicit mapping errors in the Podman debug output. The remedy is to add correct lines to /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid for your user and re-login. Second, users often confuse Podman's internal networking behavior with Docker's; both use bridge networking by default but how port mapping and user namespaces interact may differ. Test access locally to confirm forwarded host ports are reachable. Third, file ownership issues can arise after building images rootlessly because files created by the build may be mapped to subordinate UIDs; use chown on host files or adjust build context ownership where necessary. Fourth, some Compose features or third-party volume drivers may not be supported by podman-compose; test and simplify Compose files if orchestration fails. For diagnostics, podman info --debug, podman ps -a, and podman logs are your primary tools. The final takeaway: most Podman issues are fixable by verifying mappings, checking debug output, and being mindful of namespace implications on networking and storage.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Troubleshooting
Checklist: startup failures
  • Confirm /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid entries for your user
  • Re-login after edits so mappings apply to your session
  • Run podman info --debug to inspect rootless and mapping status
Networking & storage
  • Check host port binding and ensure no conflicts between user sessions
  • Be aware of ownership mapping for files created by builds or mounted volumes
Diagnostic Commands
podman info --debug, podman ps -a, podman logs <container>
Common Fix
Add subordinate UID/GID ranges and re-login; adjust ownership on host files if build artifacts are inaccessible.
Key Takeaway
Start troubleshooting with mapping checks and podman debug output; networking and ownership are the most frequent sources of friction.

screens.title: Security considerations and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Rootless containers significantly reduce the risk of privilege escalation to host root because container root is namespaced and mapped to subordinate non-root UIDs. However, rootless is not a silver bullet. You must still follow image security best practices: choose minimal base images, avoid running unnecessary privileged processes, add non-root users inside images where possible, and scan images for vulnerabilities before deploying them. Be cautious with bind mounts: mounting sensitive host paths into containers can expose host data regardless of namespace mappings. Another concrete practice is to avoid granting capabilities or using privileged mode unless you fully understand the host impact. For multi-tenant hosts, use per-user Podman sessions, enforce resource limits via cgroups, and monitor container logs for abnormal behavior. A common misconception is thinking rootless eliminates the need for vulnerability scanning or user-level access controls; it reduces one class of risk but other vectors remain. Final reflective question: when designing a runtime policy for a team, how will you combine rootless Podman with image scanning, supply chain controls, and minimal privileges to harden your deployment? Security considerations and best practices means continue image hygiene, least privilege, and supply chain checks even when using rootless podman to minimize attack vectors.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Security Best Practices
Image hygiene
Use minimal base images, build images with non-root users where possible, and run vulnerability scans before deployment.
Mounts & capabilities
Avoid mounting sensitive host paths and avoid granting extra capabilities or privileged mode unless necessary for the workload.
Multi-tenant controls
Use per-user Podman sessions, resource limits, and monitoring to reduce cross-user impact on shared systems.
Reflection

Rootless reduces host-level privilege risk, but build and runtime controls remain essential. How will you combine these controls in your environment?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will explore Podman, a daemonless container engine that runs containers as regular user processes and embraces the OCI standards. We'll show why Podman's architecture matters for security and resilience, how rootless containers limit exposure of host root, and how common workflow tasks—pulling images, running containers, building images, and using multi-service compose files—map to Podman commands. You will see a short hands-on plan you can use on a CentOS or Fedora-style system: install Podman, verify the rootless configuration, run a simple Nginx container without sudo, build an image from a Dockerfile, and deploy a compose file with podman-compose. We'll also cover the small but important system files that enable rootless mapping and common troubleshooting steps if mappings are missing. By the end you will understand the architectural contrast with Docker, have a repeatable set of commands to try in a lab, and be able to explain why running containers without a central root daemon reduces the attack surface. Think about how running containers as your own user changes how you grant privileges and manage lifecycle on multi-user systems.

Over the next screens you will develop a compact but practical skill set for working with Podman in an LFCE context. First, you'll learn to distinguish Podman's daemonless architecture from Docker's daemon-based model, and explain why that reduces a single point of failure and the daemon attack surface. Second, you'll install Podman on a Linux host, configure and verify a rootless environment using subuid and subgid mappings, and interpret the output of diagnostic commands. Third, you'll perform core container lifecycle tasks: pulling images, running containers, listing and stopping containers, removing containers and images, and executing into running containers for troubleshooting. Fourth, you'll build a container image from a Dockerfile using podman build and deploy multi-container applications with podman-compose in a rootless context. Each objective focuses on practical commands and common pitfalls so you can apply these skills in a lab or production-like environment and explain trade-offs to a systems team.

This second objectives page drills into the hands-on skills you'll practice. You'll learn to install Podman from your distribution repositories and confirm the package is present. Then you'll verify rootless readiness by checking subuid and subgid entries and running a diagnostic command that indicates whether Podman is operating in rootless mode. We'll practice the essential command set to pull an image, run a detached container, list containers, stop and remove a container, and remove images. You will also build an image from a Dockerfile and run it locally. Finally, you'll deploy a multi-service Compose file using podman-compose, practicing the same workflow many teams use when migrating from Docker. Each objective includes a practical verification step so you can show competency during an LFCE lab: produce podman info output that shows rootless true, run a rootless Nginx service reachable on a forwarded port, and successfully build and run a custom image created from a Dockerfile.

Let's make a precise comparison you can use during troubleshooting or in a design discussion. Docker uses a central daemon — dockerd — that runs as a privileged service and manages all containers for the host. Podman, in contrast, is daemonless: it runs commands that interact directly with kernel facilities and manages containers as user processes, each monitored by a small conmon helper. The practical security result is important: with Docker a vulnerability in dockerd could affect all containers and escalate privileges because dockerd runs with elevated rights. With Podman, containers run under the initiating user's namespace. That means if a container is compromised, the attacker only gains the privileges of that mapped user rather than the host root. A concrete example: on a shared developer workstation, multiple users can run their own rootless containers without a single root-owned daemon controlling them. A common misconception is that rootless equals fully safe; it's not. Rootless reduces host-level exposure, but image vulnerabilities and user-level data access can still cause harm. Your takeaway: when you argue for Podman in a secure environment, emphasize reduced attack surface and per-user isolation, but also advise continued image hygiene and least privilege practices.

Rootless containers let non-root users run containers without requiring sudo or membership in a docker group. The mechanism that makes this possible is user namespace mapping: the kernel maps a range of subordinate UIDs and GIDs to the non-root user's namespace so that processes inside the container can appear as root while the mapped UIDs on the host are non-privileged. On most distributions those mappings are configured in two files: /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid. Each line assigns a starting UID and a range to a user. A concrete example is adding the line that maps one hundred thousand UIDs to your account so Podman can map container root to those host UIDs. You will verify rootless operation with a diagnostic such as podman info --debug that reports rootless true. A common misstep is forgetting to log out and back in after editing subuid/subgid so the kernel mappings take effect for your session. Another mistake is assuming rootless always means the container runs as your host user inside; inside the container the user might still be root, but that root is namespaced and mapped to a non-root account on the host. Takeaway: subuid/subgid mapping is small to configure but vital to enable safe rootless workflows.

This screen gives you a concise install and verification process you can run during a live lab. First, install Podman from your distribution repositories using the package manager for your system. On CentOS Stream or Fedora-family systems the package is available and the install step is a single privileged command. Second, check for an entry for your username in /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid. If entries are missing, add a subordinate range for both files and re-login. Third, run the Podman diagnostic in debug mode to confirm Podman is operating rootless. That diagnostic output is your proof for a lab exercise: it will show a line indicating rootless true and display the ID mapping ranges. A practical tip is to create the subuid/subgid entries with the same numeric range for both files so mapping is symmetrical. A common troubleshooting step after editing the files is to log out and back in, because the kernel mapping information is applied at session start. Finally, if you need podman-compose later, install the package from the repository as well so you can use existing Compose files. This checklist keeps the number of steps minimal and repeatable during an exam environment.

In this walkthrough you'll see the core Podman commands you will run repeatedly. The Podman CLI is largely compatible with Docker, so workflows transfer quickly. Practically, you will pull an image from a registry, run a container detached and map a port, list running containers, stop and remove containers, and execute a shell inside a running container for inspection. An example workflow is pulling the latest nginx image, running it in detached mode with a host port forwarded to container port 80, confirming the container is running with the ps command, and using exec to run whoami inside to observe the mapped user inside the container. A common misconception is that the absence of sudo in these commands means less capability; actually, when running rootless, the container's root is namespaced to your subordinate UID range. The example code panel contains the exact commands you can paste into a lab terminal. After you practice these commands, you should be able to show a running rootless web server reachable on a forwarded host port and provide podman ps output as proof. Core Podman commands — terminal demo means podman's commands look like docker's but run under your user namespace when rootless, giving the same actions with lower host-level privileges.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Building container images is a frequent task in an LFCE lab or production pipeline. Podman supports building images from Dockerfiles with a nearly identical command to Docker, so you can reuse existing Dockerfiles. The typical flow is: create a Dockerfile, run the build command with a tag, and then run the resulting image. A concrete example included here uses a small Alpine-based image that installs cowsay and prints a message at runtime. The build is performed locally and the resulting image can be run without requiring a privileged daemon. A common misunderstanding is thinking podman build requires different Dockerfile syntax; it does not. Dockerfile directives and layers behave the same because Podman is OCI-compliant. When building rootless, be mindful of file ownership on the host; files created by build processes may be owned by mapped UIDs. The example code block is safe to paste into a lab terminal. After building, run the image to confirm behavior and then clean up images and containers to avoid leftover artifacts. This workflow demonstrates how Podman enables image creation without a persistent root process.

If your application uses multiple services defined in a docker-compose. yml file, podman-compose lets you bring those services up and down with familiar commands. Install the podman-compose package, then run podman-compose up -d to start services in detached mode and podman-compose down to stop them. The tool reads the existing Compose file and orchestrates containers using Podman rather than Docker. A concrete example is bringing up a web service and a database defined in a Compose file; podman-compose will create the necessary networks and start containers under rootless mappings if your session is configured. When working with Podman in rootless mode, you will encounter a small number of recurring setup and runtime issues. First, missing or incorrect subuid/subgid entries lead to UID mapping errors; the symptom is container creation failures or explicit mapping errors in the Podman debug output. The remedy is to add correct lines to /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid for your user and re-login. Second, users often confuse Podman's internal networking behavior with Docker's; both use bridge networking by default but how port mapping and user namespaces interact may differ. Test access locally to confirm forwarded host ports are reachable. Third, file ownership issues can arise after building images rootlessly because files created by the build may be mapped to subordinate UIDs; use chown on host files or adjust build context ownership where necessary. Fourth, some Compose features or third-party volume drivers may not be supported by podman-compose; test and simplify Compose files if orchestration fails. For diagnostics, podman info --debug, podman ps -a, and podman logs are your primary tools. The final takeaway: most Podman issues are fixable by verifying mappings, checking debug output, and being mindful of namespace implications on networking and storage.

Rootless containers significantly reduce the risk of privilege escalation to host root because container root is namespaced and mapped to subordinate non-root UIDs. However, rootless is not a silver bullet. You must still follow image security best practices: choose minimal base images, avoid running unnecessary privileged processes, add non-root users inside images where possible, and scan images for vulnerabilities before deploying them. Be cautious with bind mounts: mounting sensitive host paths into containers can expose host data regardless of namespace mappings. Another concrete practice is to avoid granting capabilities or using privileged mode unless you fully understand the host impact. For multi-tenant hosts, use per-user Podman sessions, enforce resource limits via cgroups, and monitor container logs for abnormal behavior. A common misconception is thinking rootless eliminates the need for vulnerability scanning or user-level access controls; it reduces one class of risk but other vectors remain.
